learningObjectives.title: Crime and punishment through the ages

questions.q: In Anglo-Saxon England, what was the 'wergild'?
options: A fine paid to the victim or their family as compensation for injury or death
A public execution held in the marketplace
A tax paid to the king by every household
A trial held before the royal court
questions.explain: Wergild ('man price') was compensation paid by an offender to a victim's family, its amount depending on the victim's social status.

questions.q: Trial by ordeal was effectively abolished in England after 1215 because:
options: The Pope ordered clergy to stop taking part in it
Parliament passed a law banning it
Juries were introduced by William the Conqueror
It was replaced by the Bloody Code
questions.explain: The Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 forbade priests from participating, removing the divine judgement the ordeal depended on.

questions.q: Why did William I introduce the 'murdrum' fine after 1066?
options: To deter the murder of Normans by making the whole local community pay a heavy fine
To raise money to build castles across England
To punish poaching in the royal forests
To compensate the families of executed rebels
questions.explain: The murdrum fine used Anglo-Saxon collective responsibility to protect the Norman minority, fining the hundred if a Norman was killed and the culprit not produced.

questions.q: The Norman Forest Laws are best described as an example of:
options: A 'social crime' resented by ordinary people but created to serve the ruling elite
A reform that reduced the number of capital offences
An Anglo-Saxon custom retained unchanged after 1066
A religious law enforced by the Church courts
questions.explain: The Forest Laws made hunting and gathering wood in royal forests illegal, creating new 'crimes' that many saw as unfair, illustrating how those in power define crime.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'Bloody Code'?
options: The large number of crimes punishable by death in the 18th and early 19th centuries
A code of conduct for medieval knights
The rules governing trial by combat
The system of blood feuds in Anglo-Saxon England
questions.explain: By around 1815 over 200 offences, including minor theft, carried the death penalty, using terror to deter crime.

questions.q: Transportation of convicts to Australia began in 1787-88 mainly because:
options: America was no longer available following its independence
Prisons in Britain had become overcrowded for the first time
The death penalty had just been abolished
Australia needed soldiers to defend the colony
questions.explain: After the American colonies won independence, Britain sent the First Fleet of convicts to Australia from 1787 as an alternative destination.

questions.q: Why were the Tolpuddle Martyrs transported to Australia in 1834?
options: For swearing secret oaths while forming a trade union
For leading a violent riot against factory owners
For poaching deer in a royal forest
For refusing to pay their taxes
questions.explain: The Dorset labourers were convicted under an obscure law against secret oaths, as authorities feared their agricultural trade union.

questions.q: Which reformer is most associated with improving conditions for women prisoners at Newgate Prison?
options: Elizabeth Fry
John Howard
Robert Peel
Matthew Hopkins
questions.explain: The Quaker Elizabeth Fry campaigned from 1813 to improve the treatment, education and dignity of female prisoners at Newgate.

questions.q: In which year was the death penalty for murder abolished (suspended) in Britain?
questions.explain: The Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965 suspended capital punishment for murder, made permanent in 1969.

questions.q: A prison in the 1840s houses each inmate alone in a separate cell for work, worship and sleep to prevent them corrupting one another. Which prison system is this?
options: The separate system, as used at Pentonville
The Bloody Code
The tithing system
Trial by ordeal
questions.explain: Pentonville Prison (1842) applied the separate system, isolating prisoners to encourage reflection and reform.

questions.q: What was the purpose of the 'hue and cry' in Anglo-Saxon and medieval England?
options: The whole community was expected to chase and catch a suspected criminal
A jury decided a suspect's guilt or innocence
A fine was collected from the victim's neighbours
The king's soldiers arrested wrongdoers
questions.explain: When a crime was witnessed, anyone raising the hue and cry obliged all who heard it to join the pursuit, reflecting community-based policing.

questions.q: The Bow Street Runners were set up in 1749 by:
options: Henry Fielding
Robert Peel
Charles Warren
John Howard
questions.explain: The novelist and magistrate Henry Fielding established the Bow Street Runners in London as an early organised, paid force of thief-takers.

questions.q: The Metropolitan Police Act of 1829 was introduced by which Home Secretary?
options: Robert Peel
Henry Fielding
William Gladstone
Charles Warren
questions.explain: Sir Robert Peel's Act created London's first professional, uniformed police force, whose officers became known as 'Peelers' or 'Bobbies'.

questions.q: Why were the new London police of 1829 given uniforms of blue tailcoats and top hats rather than military-style dress?
options: To reassure the public they were a civilian force, not soldiers
Because blue dye was the cheapest available
To copy the uniform of the Bow Street Runners
Because red was reserved for detectives
questions.explain: Many feared a police force would be like an army; the deliberately non-military uniform aimed to win public acceptance.

questions.q: In which year was the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) established within the Metropolitan Police?
questions.explain: The CID was formed in 1878 to provide a dedicated body of plain-clothes detectives.

questions.q: The Anglo-Saxon 'tithing' worked on the principle of:
options: Collective responsibility, with groups of men answerable for each other's behaviour
Trained professional constables patrolling towns
Trial by combat to settle disputes
Compensation paid directly to the king
questions.explain: All men over 12 belonged to a tithing of about ten who were responsible for bringing each other to court, an early form of community self-policing.

questions.q: Why did overcrowded 'rookeries' and common lodging houses make policing Whitechapel difficult?
options: They provided anonymity and hiding places for a shifting, transient population
They were guarded by the army and off-limits to police
They were located outside the Metropolitan Police district
They contained no poor people for criminals to target
questions.explain: The dense, transient population of doss houses and rookeries made it easy for offenders to disappear and hard for police to gather reliable information.

questions.q: Which division of the Metropolitan Police was responsible for policing Whitechapel?
options: H Division
K Division
The City of London Police
The Bow Street Runners
questions.explain: H Division of the Metropolitan Police was responsible for law enforcement in Whitechapel during the c1870-1900 period.

questions.q: Which Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police resigned in 1888 amid criticism over the Jack the Ripper murders?
options: Charles Warren
Frederick Abberline
Robert Peel
George Lusk
questions.explain: Sir Charles Warren resigned as Commissioner in November 1888 after criticism of the police's failure to catch the Whitechapel murderer.

questions.q: A historian wants to investigate everyday living and working conditions of ordinary families in Whitechapel around 1881. Which source would be most useful?
options: Census returns
The confessions extracted under trial by ordeal
Anglo-Saxon law codes
Forest Law records
questions.explain: Census returns record who lived in each household, their jobs, ages and origins, making them a key source for social conditions in the historic environment.
